subsystems.name: Base instruction set
subsystems.role: the mandatory integer core every RISC-V processor must implement.

subsystems.name: Standard extensions
subsystems.role: optional blocks that turn a minimal core into a practical processor.
parts: F/D — single and double precision floating point
Zi* / Z* subsets (bit manipulation, cryptography, etc.)

subsystems.name: Microarchitecture
subsystems.role: the actual hardware design; the ISA says what, not how.

subsystems.name: Custom-extension interface
subsystems.role: lets a designer bolt on accelerator instructions without breaking the standard.

subsystems.name: Verification and compliance
subsystems.role: proves the core obeys the spec before it is committed to silicon.

subsystems.name: Software stack
subsystems.role: without compilers and an OS, the core cannot be used.
parts: Linux kernel port and boot firmware
hardware abstraction layers for custom instructions

subsystems.name: Physical implementation
subsystems.role: turns register-transfer code into a manufacturable chip.
parts: floorplan, place and route, timing closure

buildSteps.title: Pick a frozen profile
buildSteps.detail: Choose the base width (32- or 64-bit) and the exact set of ratified extensions. The choice is effectively permanent once software exists, so teams lock it early and version it.

buildSteps.title: Write or configure the core
buildSteps.detail: Either license an existing core and tune its caches and pipeline depth, or write register-transfer code from scratch — the point of an open ISA is that this choice is unconstrained.

buildSteps.title: Add domain instructions
buildSteps.detail: Accelerator operations (crypto, DSP, neural-network maths) are slotted into reserved opcode space with their own registers, so ordinary RISC-V code keeps running unmodified.

buildSteps.title: Verify against the standard
buildSteps.detail: Run compliance suites, randomised instruction streams and formal proofs of the decoder and memory model; a subtle deviation only shows up years later as a compiler bug.

buildSteps.title: Prototype on an FPGA
buildSteps.detail: Before committing to a mask set, the design is run on a field-programmable array at reduced clock speed, with the compiler, kernel and drivers already booting.

buildSteps.title: Implement physically
buildSteps.detail: Synthesis, floorplan, place and route, clock-tree and power-integrity closure against the foundry's design rules, then design-rule and timing sign-off.

buildSteps.title: Tape out and bring up
buildSteps.detail: Wafers are fabricated, packaged and tested; first-silicon boot proceeds stepwise from debug access to cache to full operating system.

buildSteps.title: Characterise and produce
buildSteps.detail: Measure frequency, power and yield across process corners, then ship with a validated toolchain and long-term spec commitment.

prerequisites.why: an ISA is only words until someone can manufacture the silicon implementing it.
synthesis, place and route at modern nodes are infeasible by hand.
GCC and LLVM support means a new core gets a working C/C++ compiler almost immediately.
Linux and real-time kernels already target RISC-V, so software need not be written from zero.
extensions must stop changing, or binary software and long-lived products break.
the ecosystem is younger than the incumbents'; teams still invest heavily in their own test infrastructure.

pathway.milestone: RISC-V cores embedded as microcontrollers and as control logic inside accelerators and storage devices
pathway.unlocks: royalty-free silicon with custom instructions and no vendor lock-in.

pathway.milestone: standardised application-class profiles that run full operating systems, targeting automotive, data-centre and consumer devices
pathway.unlocks: one binary software target spanning many vendors' chips.

pathway.milestone: ratified extension families for vector and matrix maths
pathway.unlocks: competitive machine-learning and scientific computing without proprietary add-ons.

pathway.milestone: software ecosystem parity with established architectures
pathway.unlocks: porting becomes routine, which is what finally makes the open ISA a genuine default.
